Why Cities Are Warmer

A  Anyone who has walked from a park into a busy city street on a summer afternoon will have noticed the difference in temperature. Cities are typically warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. The difference is often modest during the day but can become much larger at night, when rural areas cool quickly while city streets and buildings continue to release the heat they have absorbed. On calm, clear nights, the centres of some large cities may be several degrees warmer than nearby farmland.

B  The effect was first recorded more than two hundred years ago. In the early nineteenth century, an English amateur scientist named Luke Howard compared temperature measurements taken in central London with those from the surrounding countryside and found that the city was consistently warmer, especially at night. He attributed the difference partly to the heat produced by the burning of fuel in homes and workshops. Howard is better known today for proposing the names still used to classify clouds, but his work on urban climate was equally pioneering.

C  Several factors combine to produce the effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb a large proportion of the sunlight that falls on them and store it as heat. Concrete and brick have a high capacity to store heat, which they release slowly during the evening. In addition, cities have far less vegetation than rural areas. Plants cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration, the process by which water evaporates from leaves and soil, using energy that would otherwise warm the air. Tall buildings also trap heat between them and reduce the wind that might carry it away, while vehicles, air-conditioning units and industry add heat directly.

D  The consequences can be serious. During heatwaves, high night-time temperatures prevent people's bodies from recovering from the heat of the day, and elderly people and those with certain health conditions are particularly at risk. Several severe heatwaves in recent decades have caused thousands of additional deaths in cities. Higher temperatures also increase demand for electricity for air-conditioning, which in turn releases more waste heat and, where electricity comes from fossil fuels, more greenhouse gases. Heat can also worsen air quality by speeding up the chemical reactions that form ground-level ozone.

E  Fortunately, there are many ways to reduce urban heat. One of the simplest is to make surfaces more reflective. So-called 'cool roofs', coated with white or light-coloured materials, can stay much cooler than conventional dark roofs on sunny days, lowering the temperature inside buildings. Planting trees along streets provides shade and cooling through evapotranspiration, and studies have found that neighbourhoods with more tree cover are noticeably cooler than similar areas without trees. Green roofs, covered with plants, and features such as fountains and ponds can also help.

F  These measures are particularly important because the urban heat island effect adds to the warming caused by climate change. As more of the world's population moves to cities, and as heatwaves become more frequent and intense, planning for heat is becoming as important as planning for floods or traffic. However, the benefits of cooling measures are not always shared equally. In many cities, wealthier neighbourhoods have more trees and green space than poorer ones, which means that the people with the fewest resources to cope with heat are often the most exposed to it. Some city authorities have therefore begun to target tree-planting programmes at the hottest and most deprived areas.

The Journey of Paper

A  Few inventions have had as great an influence on human culture as paper, yet its origins are surprisingly obscure. According to traditional Chinese accounts, paper was invented in 105 CE by Cai Lun, an official at the Han imperial court, who presented the emperor with a writing material made from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets. Archaeological discoveries, however, have shown that paper existed in China at least two centuries earlier. Cai Lun's real achievement was probably to improve and standardise the process rather than to invent it.

B  The basic method has remained much the same ever since. Plant fibres are soaked and beaten until they separate into a pulp, which is mixed with water. A mould, consisting of a fine screen stretched across a frame, is dipped into the mixture and lifted out, so that a thin layer of fibres is left on the screen as the water drains away. The wet sheet is then pressed and dried. At first, paper in China was used for wrapping and padding as well as for writing, but by the third and fourth centuries CE it had largely replaced bamboo strips and silk as the main writing surface.

C  Papermaking spread to Korea and Japan in the following centuries, and later westward into the Islamic world. A well-known story claims that the technique reached the city of Samarkand in Central Asia after Chinese papermakers were captured at a battle in 751 CE. Modern historians treat this account with caution, since paper was probably already known in the region through trade. What is certain is that by the end of the eighth century paper was being produced in Baghdad, and it soon became central to the administration and scholarship of the Islamic world, where it was used for government records, scientific works and copies of the Qur'an.

D  Paper reached Europe through Muslim Spain, where papermaking was established by the twelfth century. Italian papermakers in the thirteenth century introduced several important improvements, including water-powered hammers to beat the fibres, the use of animal gelatine to coat paper so that ink did not spread, and watermarks, designs pressed into the paper during manufacture that identified the mill where it was made. European paper was made almost entirely from linen and cotton rags, which were collected and sold to mills.

E  The invention of printing with movable type in Europe in the fifteenth century dramatically increased demand for paper. passage:
How Animals Sleep

A  Sleep is a strange behaviour from an evolutionary point of view. A sleeping animal is not eating, mating or watching for predators, and it may be extremely vulnerable to attack. If sleep served no essential purpose, natural selection might be expected to have eliminated it. Yet sleep, or something closely resembling it, appears to be found in almost every animal that has been carefully studied, from mammals and birds to fish, insects and even some worms. This suggests that it performs functions so important that they outweigh its risks.

B  The amount of sleep animals need varies enormously. Some bats spend up to twenty hours a day asleep, while giraffes in captivity have been recorded sleeping for less than five hours, often in short periods lasting only a few minutes. Large grazing animals in general tend to sleep relatively little, perhaps because they must spend many hours eating low-energy food and because lying down for long periods would expose them to predators. However, researchers have struggled to find any simple rule linking sleep duration to body size, diet or brain size that applies across all species.

C  Some of the most remarkable adaptations are found in animals that cannot easily stop moving. Dolphins and some other marine mammals must surface regularly to breathe, and they solve this problem by sleeping with one half of the brain at a time. During this 'unihemispheric' sleep, one eye often remains open, allowing the animal to keep watch and to stay in contact with its group. Some birds can do something similar. In a study of frigatebirds, which fly over the ocean for weeks without landing, researchers recorded brain activity during flight and found that the birds did sleep in the air, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both. However, they slept for less than an hour a day while flying, compared with more than twelve hours a day on land.

D  Even animals without a brain in the usual sense may sleep. In 2017, researchers reported that a species of jellyfish, which has a simple network of nerves but no central brain, enters a state at night in which its pulsing slows, it responds less quickly to stimuli and, if prevented from resting, it is less active the following day. These are among the criteria scientists use to define sleep, which suggests that the behaviour may have evolved very early in animal history.

E  Why sleep is so important remains a subject of active research. One leading idea is that sleep helps to consolidate memories, strengthening important connections between nerve cells and weakening less useful ones. Experiments with rats have shown that patterns of brain activity recorded while the animals learned a route through a maze were replayed during subsequent sleep. Another hypothesis emerged from studies in mice published in 2013, which suggested that during sleep the spaces between brain cells expand, allowing waste products to be cleared away more efficiently than during waking.

F  These functions are not mutually exclusive, and sleep may have acquired several roles during the course of evolution. What is clear is that its loss can have serious consequences. In laboratory animals, prolonged and complete sleep deprivation has been shown to be fatal, and in humans even moderate, long-term sleep loss is associated with impaired attention, weakened immunity and an increased risk of a range of illnesses. Studying the remarkable variety of sleep across the animal kingdom may help scientists to identify which of its functions are truly universal.

Can We Rebuild Coral Reefs?

A  Coral reefs cover well under one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are thought to support around a quarter of all marine species. They protect coastlines from waves and storms, sustain fisheries on which hundreds of millions of people depend and attract large numbers of tourists. They are also among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change. Pollution, overfishing and damage from boats and coastal construction add to the pressure, and in many places live coral cover has declined sharply over recent decades. In response, scientists and conservation groups around the world have begun to experiment with ways of actively restoring damaged reefs.

B  The principal threat is coral bleaching. Reef-building corals live in partnership with microscopic algae that inhabit their tissues and provide most of their food through photosynthesis. When the water becomes unusually warm for an extended period, this relationship breaks down and the corals expel the algae, losing their colour and turning white. Bleached corals are not dead, and if temperatures return to normal quickly they may recover, but prolonged bleaching often leads to starvation and death. Mass bleaching events, affecting reefs across entire ocean regions, have become much more frequent since the 1980s, leaving less time for reefs to recover between them.

C  The most widely used restoration method is known as coral gardening. Small fragments are cut from healthy corals and grown in underwater nurseries, often hanging from ropes or frames where they are protected from sediment and predators. Once they have grown large enough, they are attached to damaged areas of reef. Because many branching corals grow quickly and can regenerate from fragments, a single colony can provide material for many new ones without being killed.

D  Researchers have also developed techniques for slower-growing species. One of these, microfragmentation, involves cutting massive corals into very small pieces. Surprisingly, these tiny fragments grow much faster than would be expected, and when several are placed close together, they can fuse into a single colony within a few years rather than the decades normally required. Other projects collect the eggs and sperm that corals release during mass spawning events, raise the larvae in tanks and then release them onto damaged reefs.

E  Some scientists are going further, attempting to increase the heat tolerance of corals. This 'assisted evolution' may involve selectively breeding corals that have survived bleaching events, or exposing them to gradually rising temperatures so that they become more resistant. Another line of research focuses on the algae rather than the corals themselves, searching for strains that remain in partnership with their hosts at higher temperatures. Such approaches are promising but controversial, partly because of concerns that changing the genetic makeup of reef populations could have unintended consequences. Critics also worry that the promise of heat-resistant corals could reduce the pressure on governments to tackle climate change.

F  Despite these advances, the limitations of restoration are considerable. Most projects cover areas of a few hectares at most, while the world's reefs extend over hundreds of thousands of square kilometres. Restoration is also expensive, and corals planted on a reef can be lost in a single bleaching event if the underlying causes of damage remain. For this reason, most reef scientists stress that restoration cannot replace reducing greenhouse gas emissions, which is the only way to address the root cause of rising ocean temperatures.
